newsitem.title: USA: Improve small airports' firefighting - U.S. board. [CORRECTED 22:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Improve small airports' firefighting - U.S. board. [CORRECTED 22:35 GMT]

text.p: A fatal air crash at a small Midwestern airport prompted federal safety investigators on Tuesday (corrects from Monday) to urge better firefighting capability at such airfields.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) recommended that federal authorities find ways to pay for aircraft rescue and firefighting protection for commuter airline passengers on scheduled flights with 10 or more passenger seats.

Currently, such firefighting protection is required only for scheduled flights with 30 or more passenger seats, NTSB investigators said at a hearing where the recommendations were discussed and approved.
The recommendation stemmed from an investigation of a runway crash and fire at an airfield in Quincy, Illinois, last Nov. 19 in which 14 people were killed.

NTSB investigators described an accident involving three aircraft caused by a number of problems but noted, "If on-airport rescue and firefighting protection had been required for this operation at Quincy Airport, lives might have been saved."

In the Quincy accident, the investigators said, a scheduled United Express flight with 10 passengers and two crew members aboard was landing while a private plane carrying two people was taking off on an intersecting runway. The two planes crashed at the intersection.

Another small plane, flown by a pilot with only about 80 hours of experience, was waiting in a runup area behind the runway where the private plane was taxiing. Investigators said this pilot's radio transmissions might have misled the United Express pilot into believing the runway was clear.

Once the crash occurred, passengers and crew might have survived the impact if they had been able to withstand the fire that ignited almost immediately, investigators said. But there was no firefighting capability at that time at the airport, and the city's firefighters took 12 minutes to reach the site.

By that time, two people who happened to be at the airfield had reached the flaming passenger aircraft and tried to open the door nearest the cockpit but failed, the investigators said. The would-be rescuers were able to hear the pilot inside the plane as he too tried to open the door.
The pilot's body was found between the front door and an emergency door inside the plane, the investigators said.
The three planes communicated on a common radio frequency to arrange their movements, as is customary at airports like Quincy's where there is no control tower.

The board recommended that the Federal Aviation Administration ensure better pilot training for landing at such airports. It also asked for an evaluation of the door that failed to open on the United Express aircraft and of policies designed to make sure such doors will not jam.

They further urged the FAA to post on its Internet home page a list of airports that have scheduled air service but no aircraft rescue and firefighting capability. That list would include about 70 airports in the continental United States, NTSB investigators said.
The FAA is not required to comply with the board's recommendations but does in most cases, board chairman Jim Hall said.
